caseStudies.title: From Vague Accountability to Controlled Shift Handoffs
caseStudies.challenge: Shift accountability at Cala was undefined. Food runners started and ended shifts without a structured check-in or check-out. Dry storage lacked consistent signoff controls. The result was gaps in responsibility: tasks were assumed completed without verification, and problems discovered on one shift could not be traced to their origin.
caseStudies.move: Cala implemented a food-runner check-in and check-out process. Each food runner now confirms readiness at shift start and completes a structured handoff at shift end. Dry-storage signoff controls were introduced so that inventory movements are recorded and attributable. The changes created a clear chain of responsibility across shifts.
caseStudies.lesson: Accountability requires structure, not just expectation. When check-in, check-out, and signoff controls exist, responsibility becomes traceable. Vague accountability produces vague results.

caseStudies.title: Fixing Cancellation and No-Show Execution
caseStudies.challenge: Cancellations and no-shows were handled inconsistently. Confirmation at check-in was not always performed correctly. When guests cancelled, visit notes were not reliably recorded. Seating decisions after cancellations lacked shared ownership among the management team.
caseStudies.move: The team established correct confirmation procedures at check-in, ensuring every arriving party is verified against the reservation. For cancellations, managers now record visit notes documenting the cancellation and any relevant context. Seating responsibility after cancellations became a shared management function rather than falling to whoever happened to notice the empty table.
caseStudies.lesson: Reservation discipline is a system, not a reaction. Correct confirmation at check-in, documented cancellations, and shared seating responsibility prevent small gaps from compounding into lost revenue and poor guest experience.

caseStudies.title: A Process Correction for Menu Execution
caseStudies.challenge: A signature menu item was being overcooked due to the existing preparation method. The oven-based cooking process was producing inconsistent results, and the hold time between cooking and service was not protecting the quality of the finished product.
caseStudies.move: The kitchen changed the method: less oven cooking, followed by holding the item in broth at the specified temperature. The adjusted process was intended to protect texture and consistency. Approved time-and-temperature and food-safety standards still govern the procedure.
caseStudies.lesson: When a preparation method produces inconsistent results, revise the method and verify the result. Process corrections are not about blame; they are about finding a repeatable procedure and documenting it so the standard survives staff turnover.

caseStudies.title: Cross-Concept Guest Journey Thinking
caseStudies.challenge: Late-night guests at Tell Your Friends and dinner guests at The Americano operated as separate audiences with no designed connection between the two concepts, even though they share a building. The opportunity to move guests between concepts was not being captured systematically.
caseStudies.move: A Friday and Saturday reverse happy hour was designed to create a guest pathway from Tell Your Friends upstairs to The Americano. The program was structured to give late-night TYF guests a reason to transition to the Americano dining experience. This is an example of cross-concept guest-journey thinking: designing an operating connection between two venues rather than treating them as independent.
caseStudies.lesson: When multiple concepts share proximity, the guest journey between them is a design problem, not an accident. Strategic operating connections between venues can serve guests better than treating each concept as isolated. This remains a strategic operating example; outcomes depend on continued execution.

caseStudies.title: Managing a Major Menu Transition
caseStudies.challenge: A significant menu transition required coordination across manager logs, staff training, revised service standards, and operating stabilization. The scope of the change meant that multiple systems needed to update simultaneously, and the risk of inconsistency during the transition period was high.
caseStudies.move: The management team used structured manager logs to track the transition. Training sessions covered the new menu items and revised service standards. Operating stabilization became an explicit goal with defined checkpoints rather than an assumed outcome. The transition is being managed as an ongoing process with active monitoring.
caseStudies.lesson: Major menu transitions are operating projects, not just kitchen events. They require manager logs, training plans, revised service standards, and explicit stabilization checkpoints. Treating a menu change as a one-day event creates weeks of inconsistency.

caseStudies.title: Unknown Stays Unknown Until the Data Exists
caseStudies.challenge: Polished-looking reports were being produced even when current-period source data was incomplete or missing. The reports looked authoritative but could not be verified against actual operating numbers. The risk was that decisions would be made on partial information presented as complete.
caseStudies.move: The reporting standard was changed: when current-period source data is missing, the report now explicitly marks that data as unknown rather than filling gaps with estimates or prior-period numbers. Missing data blocks the production of a polished report until the source information is available.
caseStudies.lesson: Management integrity means unknown stays unknown. A report that looks complete but contains unverifiable numbers is worse than no report at all, because it creates false confidence. The discipline is to surface gaps rather than paper over them.
